Key Research Thinking Patterns: Combinatorial-Geometric Reduction: Translating complex topological structures into discrete combinatorial models to enable algorithmic analysis and classification (e.g., Using Bass-Serre trees and graph of groups decompositions to classify Generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups and their splittings).

Optimization-Based Invariant Computation: Applying linear programming techniques to compute geometric invariants and establish rationality properties of topological norms (e.g., Computing Stable Commutator Length via linear programming reduction on extremal surfaces encoded by taut surfaces).

Spectral-Geometric Parametrization: Utilizing analytic function theory to characterize the topology of spectral spaces and solve inverse problems for canonical systems (e.g., Employing Titchmarsh-Weyl m-functions and Krein function parametrizations to show spectral spaces are homeomorphic to products of disks and tori).

Algebraic-Topological Invariant Analysis: Leveraging algebraic structures like trace fields and quaternion algebras to distinguish commensurability classes and isometry groups of manifolds (e.g., Analyzing invariant trace fields and quaternion algebras to classify minimal complexity hyperbolic 3-manifolds and construct incommensurable lattices).
Summary Description: Max Forester is a mathematician specializing in Geometric Group Theory, Geometric Topology, and Spectral Theory. His research bridges combinatorial group structures with hyperbolic geometry and functional analysis. He employs Bass-Serre theory and deformation spaces to classify group splittings and Generalized Baumslag-Solitar groups, while utilizing linear programming to compute stable commutator length and analyze extremal surfaces. In the realm of 3-manifolds, he investigates commensurability invariants and minimal complexity triangulations. More recently, Forester has extended into inverse spectral theory, using Titchmarsh-Weyl m-functions and Krein parametrizations to characterize the topology of reflectionless canonical systems. His work demonstrates a rigorous synthesis of discrete combinatorial methods and continuous analytic techniques to solve fundamental classification problems in geometry and topology.
